transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Um, hi. Yeah, I came in because... well, it's about my eating. It's gotten really bad. Basically, once I start eating, it feels like I just disappear, you know? Like something else entirely takes over. 

It actually feels a lot like what happened to my car last week when the steering column locked up on the highway. I was trying to turn the wheel and it just wouldn't budge, which was terrifying because I was on my way to campus. I'm taking a few classes right now—well, I was, I've missed a lot of them lately. My history professor is just so strict about attendance, he literally locks the lecture hall door at exactly 9:05. If you're late, you're just stuck in the hallway. 

But anyway, with the food, it's exactly like that locked steering wheel. Even while I am actively telling myself to stop, like my brain is screaming at me to just put the food down, I can't. I just keep going and going until I physically can't stand it anymore. It's just... I don't know. Did you ever have to take those massive history prerequisites? Probably not, you went to med school. But yeah, the not being able to stop thing... that's why I'm here.
After you've had one of these episodes where you feel like you can't stop eating, do you ever try to compensate for it by making yourself vomit, using laxatives, or exercising excessively?

Yeah, I... I do. After I eat like that, I usually end up in a bathroom in the dorm or, like, a quiet floor of the library, making myself throw up. I just get so terrified that all that food is just sitting in my stomach turning into weight. 

But honestly, finding a quiet bathroom on campus is way harder than it sounds. I usually go to the fourth floor of the library because it's the archives section, and nobody ever goes up there except this one older librarian. She always wears these really loud, clunky heels, so you can hear her coming from a mile away. It echoes so badly up there now because they took out all the carpet over the summer. I have absolutely no idea why they did that, the carpet was totally fine, and now the whole building just feels cold and echoes whenever anyone even drops a pen. I read in the student paper that they spent like a million dollars on the renovation, which is crazy when our dorm heating barely works. My roommate has been sleeping in a winter coat since October. He actually tried to petition the housing office about it, but they just sent him an automated email... wait, what were you asking me about?
How often do you experience these episodes where you feel like you can't stop eating followed by making yourself vomit?

Um, how often... well, for most of this semester, it's been happening several times a week. It's not just a once-in-a-while thing anymore. Like, if I look back over at least the last few months, there really hasn't been a single week where the whole cycle stopped. It's just constant. 

Especially since they changed the dining hall hours this semester. They used to be open until midnight, but now they close at 8 PM, which is ridiculous because who eats dinner that early? So everyone ends up ordering delivery, and there are constantly dozens of greasy paper bags piling up in the dorm lobby. The front desk guy, Dave, gets so insanely mad about the trash. Dave is actually a grad student, I think he's studying marine biology or something, which makes absolutely no sense because we are in a landlocked state. Like, the closest ocean is at least a twelve-hour drive. Why would you come here for marine biology? He has this giant fish tank behind the front desk, though, with these really aggressive neon fish that just chase each other around all day. I was watching them for like twenty minutes yesterday while waiting for my roommate to bring his keys down, and they literally never stop moving. It's kind of exhausting just looking at them. 

But anyway, wait... sorry. What did you ask me? Oh, right, the frequency. Yeah, multiple times a week for the last few months. It just hasn't stopped.

During these episodes where you feel like you can't stop eating, would you say that you feel a complete loss of control over how much you're eating, like you're unable to stop yourself once you start?

Yeah, exactly. Like I was trying to explain when I first came in, it's a total loss of control. Once I start eating, it's like I just disappear and something else takes over completely. Even though my brain is actively screaming at me to stop, I just keep going and going until I physically can't stand it anymore. 

It's honestly like being on autopilot, or... you know how people talk about the algorithm taking over your brain? My roommate will sit on his bed scrolling his phone for literally four hours straight. He just zones out completely. I was trying to talk to him yesterday while he was watching this endless loop of people pressure-washing driveways. Which, I mean, is oddly satisfying, I get the appeal. There's this one account that does it in time to 80s synth-pop, and the guy has like two million followers just for cleaning concrete. 

But my roommate was so checked out he didn't even hear the fire alarm testing they did in our hall. Our RA, Sarah, had to physically bang on our door to make sure we were evacuating. Sarah takes her job way too seriously, honestly. She wrote a guy on our floor up last week because his boots were technically two inches out into the hallway. She carries around this little clipboard everywhere she goes, even to the dining hall. It's pretty intense, like she thinks she's the dorm police or something. 

But... yeah, sorry. What you said. Total loss of control. I just can't stop myself once I start.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms of recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by compensatory behaviors (self-induced vomiting), occurring multiple times a week over several months, along with a sense of lack of control during eating episodes, strongly aligns with the diagnostic criteria for bulimia nervosa (F50.2). Other candidates (F50.0, F50.9, F42) are ruled out based on current information.

inference_history.note: The patient described a loss of control during eating episodes, suggesting possible binge eating disorder (F50.2). Anorexia nervosa (F50.0) is considered due to the broad category of eating disorders, though no restriction or weight concerns are explicitly mentioned yet. Eating disorder, unspecified (F50.9) is included as a differential until more details clarify the exact nature of the disturbance. OCD (F42) is considered due to the theme of perceived lack of control despite internal resistance, though more information is needed to confirm obsessive or compulsive elements.
